title: Glorious Revolution
description: 1688 deposition of James II of England
wiki_lead:
The Glorious Revolution was the deposition of King James II of England in November 1688. He was replaced by his daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband, James's nephew William III of Orange. The two ruled as joint monarchs of England, Scotland, and Ireland until Mary's death in 1694, when William became ruler in his own right. Jacobitism, the political movement that aimed to restore the exiled James or his descendants of the House of Stuart to the throne, persisted into the late 18th century. Some historians consider William's invasion the last successful invasion of England.
Despite being a Roman Catholic, James had become king in February 1685 with widespread backing from the Protestant majorities in England and Scotland, as well as largely Catholic Ireland, but his policies quickly eroded support. The prospect of a Catholic dynasty following the birth of his son James Francis Edward Stuart on 10 June 1688 led some of his domestic opponents to issue the Invitation to William, seeking Dutch support to remove him.
The Dutch States General and William of Orange were concerned that James might support France in the Nine Years' War. Exploiting unrest in England and claiming to be responding to the invitation, William landed with an army in Devon on 5 November 1688. As William advanced on London, James's army disintegrated and he went into exile in France on 23 December. In April 1689, a Convention made William and Mary joint monarchs of England and Ireland. A separate but similar Scottish settlement was made in June 1689. 
Domestically, the Revolution formally established constitutional monarchy as the British form of government, while the Dutch Republic and Britain became allies in resisting French expansion, an arrangement which persisted for much of the 18th century.

Background

Despite his personal Catholicism, James became king in February 1685 with widespread backing in all three of his kingdoms, leading to the swift crushing of Protestant uprisings in both Scotland and England. However, James failed to appreciate the extent to which his power relied on support from the landed gentry, whose alienation fatally damaged his regime. The vast majority of the gentry in England and Scotland were Protestant, while even in largely Catholic Ireland a disproportionate number were members of the Protestant Church of Ireland. His supporters accepted James's personal religious beliefs, so long as he maintained the primacy of the Protestant Church of England and Church of Scotland. When his policies appeared to undermine them, it destabilised all three kingdoms.

grok_lead: The Glorious Revolution of 1688â1689 entailed the overthrow of the Catholic King James II of England, Scotland, and Ireland through an invasion by his Protestant nephew and son-in-law, William III, Prince of Orange, at the behest of English political and religious leaders alarmed by James's absolutist tendencies and efforts to advance Catholicism. James's policies, including the suspension of anti-Catholic laws via the Declaration of Indulgence and the birth of a male heir in June 1688âraising fears of a perpetual Catholic dynastyâprompted seven prominent figures, known as the Immortal Seven, to invite William to intervene on 30 June 1688. William landed at Brixham in Devon on 5 November with a Dutch force of about 15,000 men, facing minimal resistance as James's army fragmented through desertions and defections. James fled to France in December, paving the way for Parliament to declare the throne vacant and offer it jointly to William and his wife Mary II, James's Protestant daughter, conditional on their acceptance of constitutional limits. Though celebrated as "glorious" for its largely non-violent character in Englandâcontrasting with the bloodshed of prior upheavals like the English Civil War âthe event entrenched parliamentary sovereignty and curtailed monarchical powers via the Bill of Rights 1689, which prohibited suspending laws without consent, required frequent parliaments, enshrined free elections and speech in Parliament, and barred Catholics from the throne. This settlement marked a pivotal shift toward constitutional monarchy, influenced by Whig and Tory elites prioritizing Protestant succession and resistance to perceived absolutism, while William sought to counter French expansion under Louis XIV by securing Britain's alliance. Controversies persist over its revolutionary nature, with some historians viewing it as a negotiated elite compact rather than popular upheaval, and others emphasizing its role in fostering financial innovations like the Bank of England to fund wars against France. The revolution ignited Jacobite resistance in Scotland and Ireland, where James's supporters challenged William's rule, underscoring uneven acceptance across the realms.
